title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Marine
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: North Carolina Ports hit by intrusion that took cargo processing systems offline across three facilities
items.content_text: The North Carolina State Ports Authority detected an unauthorised intrusion on 4 August that triggered a systems-wide IT outage across all three of its maritime logistics hubs: the Port of Wilmington, the Port of Morehead City and the Charlotte Inland Port. Processing workflows were directly affected, with truck movements, cargo processing and administrative systems disrupted while restoration was underway. Terminal operations and vessel activity continued as scheduled, and some cargo processing shifted to manual handling. The incident is a clean illustration of a pattern this sector keeps repeating: the ships kept moving and the cranes kept working, but the paperwork layer that tells the terminal what to move and releases it to a trucker went down, and that is enough to back up a gate queue and ripple into inland rail-served facilities.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: North Carolina State Ports Authority — reported by Splash247 and Cybernews

items.title: CEVA Logistics breach affects European warehouses and spills customer data through its retail clients
items.content_text: CEVA Logistics, one of the world’s largest shipping and logistics operators, was attacked between 29 July and 1 August, with the intrusion affecting at least eight warehouses across Europe. The France-headquartered company runs more than a thousand warehouses worldwide and reported 18.3 billion dollars in revenue last year. The consequences surfaced indirectly: several companies that rely on CEVA for fulfilment disclosed that their customers’ personal information was taken in the breach, including Dutch e-commerce group Bol, department store De Bijenkorf, eyewear company Ace & Tate, football club Ajax, and Steam’s European hardware business. For marine and port operators the lesson is about position in the chain rather than the specific victim: a third-party logistics provider holds consignee data, routing detail and warehouse operations for hundreds of shippers at once, so one compromise produces notification obligations across a long list of unrelated customers.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: TechCrunch, corroborated by The Record and The Register

items.title: Five federal agencies warn AI-written scripts are reading Siemens S7 controllers, commercial facilities in scope
items.content_text: The NSA, CISA, FBI, Department of Energy and EPA issued a joint advisory on 19 August warning that threat actors are combining the open-source snap7 and python-snap7 libraries with AI-assisted scripting to build tools that mimic legitimate OT monitoring software, giving read and write access to Siemens S7 controller memory, configuration data and ladder logic over S7comm. Critical manufacturing, energy, water, chemical, food and agriculture, and commercial facilities are named as the most-targeted sectors. Actors locate exposed devices using internet scanning services and gain access through default or weakly configured credentials rather than a vulnerability. Affected lines span the S7-200, S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 and S7-1500 including F-series safety controllers. Shoreside terminals are squarely inside the commercial facilities scope: S7 and comparable controllers run bulk and conveyor handling, shore power, fuelling systems, gate barriers and terminal building services, and many were commissioned by an integrator with remote access still enabled.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Joint advisory AA26-231A (NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE, EPA) — corroborated by SecurityWeek and Help Net Security

items.title: Industrial ransomware rose 12 percent in Q2, and disrupted output without touching control systems
items.content_text: Dragos recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents at industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up from 1,020 in the first quarter, with manufacturing accounting for 747, construction 176, equipment manufacturing 114 and food and beverage 70. The finding most relevant to ports and vessel operators concerns mechanism rather than sector counts: disrupting the IT systems supporting an industrial environment is regularly sufficient to interrupt operations even when attackers never reach the control system, and extortion continued shifting from file encryption toward data theft. The North Carolina Ports outage is a textbook instance — cranes and berths unaffected, cargo processing halted. For vessel operators the equivalent exposure sits in fleet management, planned maintenance, crewing and charter systems ashore, whose loss disrupts commercial operation long before anything on the bridge is at risk.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Dragos Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis — via Help Net Security

items.title: Claroty finds one in five facility cyber-physical assets a single hop from internet-exposed systems
items.content_text: Team82 analysed more than 750,000 cyber-physical assets across major data centre facilities and found nearly one in five sitting one hop from a system making outbound internet connections. Close to 90 percent of the building management systems examined communicated over insecure protocols and 40 percent ran outdated firmware, with around a third of HVAC and cooling systems one hop from an internet-exposed system. The research is about data centres, but the asset classes are the same ones a port authority or terminal operator runs: power distribution units, building management, physical access control, fire protection and cooling. The methodology transfers cleanly — count the hops from any internet-facing system to the controllers governing reefer power, gatehouse access control and terminal building services, and most operators have never measured it.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Claroty Team82, State of CPS Security: Data Center Exposures — reported by SecurityWeek

items.title: Cisco ASA and FTD VPN zero-day exploited to reload firewalls, added to CISA KEV
items.content_text: Cisco has patched CVE-2026-20349, a flaw in the remote-access SSL VPN service of Secure Firewall ASA and Secure Firewall Threat Defense software that attackers are exploiting to force appliances offline. A specially crafted HTTP request to the vulnerable service causes an unexpected reload and a denial-of-service condition, requiring no authentication and no user interaction. Cisco’s PSIRT confirmed active exploitation in August, and CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue with a federal remediation deadline of 14 August. Hot fixes cover ASA 9.16, 9.18, 9.20, 9.22, 9.23 and 9.24 and FTD 7.0, 7.2, 7.4, 7.6, 7.7 and 10.0. In a maritime context these appliances typically terminate the links carrying vendor support into terminal systems, shore-to-ship connectivity, and remote access for staff at inland and satellite facilities — so an attacker can remove your remote support path at the moment you most need it.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Cisco security advisory and CISA KEV catalogue — reported by Help Net Security and SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Exploitation confirmed and KEV listed Aug 2026; reported 13 Aug 2026

items.title: August ICS Patch Tuesday: maximum-severity missing authentication in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced
items.content_text: Siemens published ten advisories in the August cycle. The most severe, SSA-834709, is a maximum-severity missing authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker execute arbitrary code on the underlying server with elevated privileges. Siemens also fixed a critical code execution vulnerability in Siveillance Video Management Servers and high-severity flaws in Solid Edge, Simcenter Nastran, Siemens License Server, Simcenter Femap, Parasolid and Logo! Soft Comfort, with medium-severity issues in Ruggedcom devices and Desigo controllers. Schneider Electric published advisories for NetBotz 5 and PowerChute Serial Shutdown, and Phoenix Contact one covering multiple PLCnext firmware flaws. Two of these land squarely in port estates: Siveillance is a video management platform widely deployed for terminal and perimeter surveillance under facility security plans, and Ruggedcom switches are common in harsh-environment terminal and quayside networks.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Siemens ProductCERT SSA-834709, Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact advisories — summarised by SecurityWeek

items.title: Four more exploited flaws added to KEV on 18 August, including Windows IKE and VMware vCenter
items.content_text: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August: CVE-2026-33824 in Microsoft Internet Key Exchange, CVE-2026-55040 in Microsoft SharePoint, CVE-2026-59310 in Broadcom VMware vCenter and CVE-2026-65400 in Apple macOS. Two further additions followed on 20 August, both in TrueConf Server. For port and vessel operators the IKE and vCenter entries carry the most weight. IKE terminates the site-to-site tunnels linking terminals, inland facilities and headquarters, and frequently the shore end of vessel connectivity. vCenter typically manages the virtual infrastructure hosting terminal operating systems, berth planning and historians — a compromise there is a hypervisor-level problem affecting everything running on it. SharePoint is worth a second look in this sector specifically because facility and vessel security plan documentation, procedures and drawings are so often stored there.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Added 18 Aug 2026; two further additions 20 Aug 2026

items.title: CISA publishes an advisory for flaws in Malcolm, its own free OT monitoring suite
items.content_text: Advisory ICSA-26-230-01 covers vulnerabilities in Malcolm, the network traffic analysis suite CISA distributes free for OT and ICS environments, which could let an attacker cause a denial-of-service condition or execute arbitrary code. Affected versions are below 26.06.1, below 26.07.0 and up to and including 26.07.1. On the same day CISA published ICSA-26-230-02, a stack overflow in Siemens Simcenter Nastran that can lead to remote code execution if a user is tricked into running the affected binary with a malicious string; Siemens has released fixed versions. Malcolm turns up more often in this sector than expected, because smaller port authorities and terminal operators without a commercial OT monitoring budget deploy it to satisfy visibility expectations under the Coast Guard rule — typically on a span or tap seeing the whole terminal network, and typically outside the patch inventory.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-230-01 and ICSA-26-230-02

items.title: Coast Guard cyber rule: annual training already required, Cybersecurity Plans due 16 July 2027
items.content_text: The Coast Guard’s Cybersecurity in the Marine Transportation System rule, codified at 33 CFR Part 101 Subpart F, took effect on 16 July 2025 and applies to owners and operators of US-flagged vessels, Outer Continental Shelf facilities and facilities regulated under the Maritime Transportation Security Act. Two dates govern current planning. Personnel training required under 33 CFR 101.650 has been mandatory since 12 January 2026 and recurs annually. The substantive deadline is 16 July 2027, by which point owners and operators must have designated a Cybersecurity Officer, conducted a Cybersecurity Assessment, and submitted a Cybersecurity Plan to the Coast Guard for review and approval. The Coast Guard has also signalled increased Port State Control attention to poor cybersecurity practice, where findings can produce deficiencies, detention, denial of entry or Captain of the Port restrictions on vessel movement.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: US Coast Guard final rule, Federal Register — codified at 33 CFR Part 101 Subpart F
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Rule effective 16 Jul 2025; training since 12 Jan 2026; plans due 16 Jul 2027

items.title: US and Australian agencies publish guidance on isolating OT and operating that way for an extended period
items.content_text: A joint publication from US and Australian agencies sets out how critical infrastructure operators should prepare to isolate vital operational technology and supporting systems from external connectivity, and to keep operating in that isolated state for an extended period rather than the few hours most continuity plans assume. It is guidance, not a requirement. Its value in a maritime context is that it converts a claim most terminals make confidently — that they can work cargo on paper if systems go down — into a dependency checklist covering time synchronisation, authentication, licence servers, customs and cargo release interfaces, and the physical availability of staff who have done it before. The North Carolina Ports incident is a live example of the scenario: terminal operations continued while processing shifted to manual, and the constraint was documentation flow rather than machinery.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Joint US–Australian OT isolation guidance — reported by SecurityWeek
